17.1.8 Substitution versus Elimination

We have studied that an alkyl halide and a Lewis base can react together in either a substitution or an elimination reaction (Section 17.1.5). Substitution and elimination reactions are very often in competition with each other. Two important factors i.e. nature of alkyl halide and nature of Lewis base, play a key role in deciding whether a principal reaction would be elimination or substitution.

Crowding around the α–carbon in molecule of substrate generally favours elimination over substitution reaction. This is due to the greater steric hindrance when the nucleophile approaches towards α–carbon atom of the substrate. Thus, greater number of alkyl groups on the substrate favours elimination over substitution because these alkyl groups stabilize the alkene more than the substitution product.

As all the bases are also nucleophiles, the competition between substitution and elimination reactions is determined by the fact whether it is a better base or a better nucleophile. A stronger base will favour elimination while a stronger nucleophile will favour substitution in the same substrate. For example, 2–bromopropane on reaction with ethoxide ion (C₂H₅O⁻) undergoes elimination and produces alkene as the major product because ethoxide is a strong base (by products are not shown).

On the other hand the same 2–bromopropane on reaction with ethanthiolate ion (C₂H₅S⁻) undergoes substitution reaction because it is more nucleophilic and less basic than ethoxide ion.

sections.content:
In a fast second step, a base abstracts a proton from the carbon atom adjacent to the positive carbon (β-carbon). These reactions are usually followed by tertiary alkyl halides, like SN1 reactions. For example, reaction of tert-butyl bromide with water, upon β-elimination yield isobutylene.

Step–1: The first step is similar to SN1 (Section 17.1.6.3)

Step–2: The base abstracts β-hydrogen of carbocation and yield isobutylene.

Because the rate-limiting step involves unimolecular ionization of the alkyl halide, the rate equation is first-order. The rate depends only on the concentration of the alkyl halide and not on the concentration of the base. rate = k [R–X] or rate = k [(CH₃)₃C–Br]

17.1.7.3 E2 Mechanism

This is a bimolecular elimination process, with both the base and the alkyl halide participating in the transition state, so this mechanism is abbreviated E2 for Elimination, bimolecular. These are generally followed by primary alkyl halides. These reactions are completed in one step like SN2 reactions.

For example, reaction of ethyl bromide with hydroxide ion to form ethene follow E2 mechanism. The removal of proton from the β-carbon atom by hydroxide base and the removal of bromide ion from the α-carbon atom takes place simultaneously.

Reaction is first order with respect to each reactant, and second order overall. rate = k[substrate] [base] or rate = k [CH₃CH₂Br][⁻OH]

Table 17.3 Summary of Elimination Reactions in Alkyl Halides

17.1.8 Substitution versus Elimination

We have studied that an alkyl halide and a Lewis base can react together in either a substitution or an elimination reaction (Section 17.1.5). Substitution and elimination reactions are very often in competition with each other. Two important factors i.e. nature of alkyl halide and nature of Lewis base, play a key role in deciding whether a principal reaction would be elimination or substitution.

Crowding around the α–carbon in molecule of substrate generally favours elimination over substitution reaction. This is due to the greater steric hindrance when the nucleophile approaches towards α–carbon atom of the substrate. Thus, greater number of alkyl groups on the substrate favours elimination over substitution because these alkyl groups stabilize the alkene more than the substitution product.

As all the bases are also nucleophiles, the competition between substitution and elimination reactions is determined by the fact whether it is a better base or a better nucleophile. A stronger base will favour elimination while a stronger nucleophile will favour substitution in the same substrate. For example, 2–bromopropane on reaction with ethoxide ion (C₂H₅O⁻) undergoes elimination and produces alkene as the major product because ethoxide is a strong base (by products are not shown).

On the other hand the same 2–bromopropane on reaction with ethanthiolate ion (C₂H₅S⁻) undergoes substitution reaction because it is more nucleophilic and less basic than ethoxide ion.
